mnemonic: A traffic cop hands back the wallet you dropped, and the thanks is already built into the word: คุณ khun means you, so khàawp-khun is thanks-you, and the cop is standing right there to collect it. Palms together, head down, the first syllable sitting low. (▁ khàawp drops low, then khun levels out flat and mid)
headline: Khàawp-khun.
scene: A Bangkok street corner in the rain. A traffic policeman in a white helmet holds out a battered leather wallet to a young woman, who has stopped mid-step and pressed her palms together in front of her face, head bowed, beaming.

mnemonic: A man backing out of a café swings his bag into a waiter and a whole rack of toast goes up in the air. On the sill a crow caws. Caw, toast. He turns round with both hands raised, wincing, saying it twice over: khǎaw-thôot. (↑ khǎaw climbs like the crow, then thôot drops as he bows)
headline: Khǎaw-thôot!
scene: The doorway of a small café. A man in a raincoat has just knocked a waiter's tray and slices of toast hang in the air around them both. He is turned back toward the waiter, shoulders hunched, both hands raised in apology, face screwed up.

mnemonic: A cow leans over the fence into the neighbour's rye field and moos, while the farmer stands beside it with his watch open, waiting on the crop. Moo, rye. mûuea-rài asks the only thing either of them wants to know: when. Say MOO with the lips pulled wide instead of pushed forward and the Thai vowel lands. (↓ mûuea drops, then rài falls away low)
headline: mûuea-rài?
scene: A brown cow with its head stretched over a wooden fence into a tall golden field of rye, mouth open mid-bellow.

mnemonic: He plunges both hands into the mountain stream and they go numb in seconds, that shocking cold where the fingers stop belonging to you. náam is water, and water this cold numbs. Short and high, up where the gasp is. (▲ high and taut, the sound of breath sucked in)
headline: náam!
scene: A young man crouched at the edge of a fast mountain stream, both hands submerged to the wrist in clear rushing water, face screwed up and mouth open in a gasp.

mnemonic: A rented room in a Hong Kong tower block, so small that a man standing in the middle of it reaches both walls without straightening his arms. Hong, hâawng: the room. This one is all the room there is, and the voice drops like the ceiling. (↓ falling, heavy and low)
headline: hâawng.
scene: A tiny high-rise flat. A man stands in the centre with both arms half raised, palms flat against opposite walls, a folded bed and a single hotplate crammed in behind him.

mnemonic: A single yen coin has been left in the freezer overnight and comes out furred with white frost, so cold it sticks to the fingertips that lift it. yen is cold, and the temperature never shifts while the voice holds it. (— flat and level, the cold does not move)
headline: yen.
scene: A close view of a hand holding a small coin, its face lost under white frost, fingertips pink and stuck to its surface, cold vapour spilling down from an open freezer behind.

mnemonic: Take royal and drop the -al: a-roy. A king in full robes has folded himself onto a plastic stool at a noodle cart, taken one mouthful and closed his eyes. The royal verdict on street food, and the whole court leaning in to watch him give it. (▁ the last syllable drops low and satisfied)
headline: à-ròi!
scene: A king in an embroidered robe and gold circlet perched on a low plastic stool at a night-market noodle cart, eyes closed in bliss, a laden spoon halfway to his mouth. The vendor grins over her steaming pot; two courtiers in uniform wait awkwardly behind.

mnemonic: ใกล้ klâi and ไกล klai are the same handful of sounds and only the tone separates them. The falling one is the one that comes down to you: a bird dropping onto an outstretched hand. The level one keeps going, out to the horizon. Near falls. Far stays flat. (↓ falling, the bird lands on the hand)
headline: klâi.
scene: A woman standing in an open field with one arm held out, a small bird just settling onto her fingers, wings still spread. Far behind her a second bird is a tiny speck against a pale sky above distant hills.

mnemonic: Say the first syllable of plaza and stop there: plah. A silver fish the length of a man has come up out of the fountain in the town plaza and is flapping about on the flagstones while the whole square backs away from it. plaa is the fish. (— flat and level, said plainly)
headline: plaa!
scene: A paved town square at midday with an ornate fountain at its centre. An enormous silver fish lies flapping on the wet flagstones beside it, water spreading around it, spray still falling.

mnemonic: The bride has lost hers somewhere in a reception of two hundred guests, so she calls across the room. One man stands up in the middle of the tables, hand high, thumb jabbing at his own chest: saa, ME. A long open aah, then ME. That is the husband. (↑ sǎa climbs as the hand goes up, then mii sits flat)
headline: saa— ME.
scene: A crowded wedding reception. A bride in white stands on a chair scanning the room, and among the seated guests one man in a dinner jacket has risen, one hand high, the other thumb pointed at his own chest, grinning.

skip_reason: The ɯa diphthong has no English match: new and gnu add a glide and drop the second half, and a noodle-bowl scene would teach the wrong meaning.

mnemonic: She lifts a tiny gold ring off the velvet and the jeweller calmly builds the stack of banknotes it will cost beside it, a stack taller than the ring is wide. The pang goes straight through her chest. phaaeng: expensive. (— flat and level, the price is not negotiable)
headline: phaaeng.
scene: A jeweller's counter under bright spotlights. A small gold ring sits on a velvet pad; beside it the jeweller has built a tall stack of banknotes. The customer has one hand pressed flat to her chest, leaning back, eyes wide.

mnemonic: The doctor tips a spoonful of syrup into the boy and, before he has finished swallowing, is already filling the spoon again. More. More rest, more water, more of this. mǎaw is the doctor, and more is what she always wants. (↑ rising, the voice lifts with the spoon)
headline: mǎaw: more.
scene: A small clinic room. A doctor in a white coat with a stethoscope round her neck holds a brimming spoon of dark syrup toward a boy on the examination couch, the bottle in her other hand already tilted to refill it.

mnemonic: The lifeboat is going down by the stern, so over the side go the suitcases, the chairs, the oars, everything. What he will not let go of is one dented tin can of water held hard against his chest. Some can. sǎm-khan is the thing that actually matters. (↑ sǎm climbs, then khan lands flat and certain)
headline: sǎm-khan.
scene: An overloaded wooden lifeboat low in a grey swell. A man at the stern heaves a suitcase over the side with one arm while the other clamps a dented tin can tight against his chest. Other passengers cling to the gunwales, soaked.

skip_reason: No single anchor for diaw-kan: duo has the wrong vowel, and assembling it from pieces takes a chain of two puns.

mnemonic: The chow bell goes at the end of harvest and the whole village comes: grandmothers, farmhands, babies on hips, every last one of them holding a bowl. ชาว is not a crowd, it is the folk of a place, the people of somewhere, and chow brings all of them out at once. (— flat and level, one long even call)
headline: chaao!
scene: A village clearing at dusk with a long trestle of steaming pots. A hundred villagers of every age converge on it from the fields and houses, bowls in hand, some running, an old woman carried between two grandsons.

mnemonic: The fairground strongman brings the mallet down and the puck goes all the way up the tower: the bell at the top rang, and rang loud enough to stop the music. แรง is that. Force, power, the strength that made the bell speak. (— flat and level, held like a struck note)
headline: …and it RANG.
scene: A night fairground high striker. A heavily built man in a vest has just swung a mallet onto the pad, the puck streaking up the tower, and the brass bell at the top is jolting sideways mid-strike.

mnemonic: Say the first syllable of kayak and stop there: kǎai. A river trader has eight of them roped nose to tail along the bank and is holding a ninth over his head, shouting across the water at the tourists. Whatever he has, he sells it. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the arms)
headline: kǎai!
scene: A muddy riverbank lined with brightly painted kayaks roped nose to tail. A wiry trader in shorts stands on an upturned hull holding one small kayak above his head with both arms, shouting across the water toward a group of tourists on the far bank. Hot bright midday, brown river.

mnemonic: Mum points, arm dead straight, at the place where the two walls meet, and the boy goes and stands in it. That exact meeting of two walls is the mum: the corner, the angle. Nobody argues with the arm. (— flat and level, no rise, no give)
headline: mum.
scene: A plain sitting room. A woman stands with her arm extended rigidly toward the corner where two walls meet; a small boy trudges toward it with his head down and one sock falling. Afternoon light through net curtains, an armchair pushed aside.

skip_reason: rá-yá has no English anchor — raja has the wrong medial consonant — and the meaning is too abstract to force a scene.

mnemonic: Sue stands in the middle of the room and the room comes to her: the rug rucking up, the chairs walking on their legs, an orange rolling across the boards. Everything goes to Sue. sùu is that word and nothing more. To, towards, into. (▁ low and flat, a short word that only points)
headline: …sùu Sue.
scene: A living room where the furniture is sliding across the floorboards toward a woman standing calmly in the centre, arms at her sides. A rug rucks up at her feet, two chairs tilt toward her mid-slide, an orange rolls across the boards.

mnemonic: The doctor asks which one is hurting and he smacks his own knee twice, hard: nîi. This one. Not that one, not the one from last year, this knee, the one he can reach and hit. นี่ always points at whatever is nearest to hand. (↓ falling, the voice drops with the hand)
headline: Nîi.
scene: A clinic examination room. A man sitting on the couch with both trouser legs rolled up slaps his own left knee with a flat palm, caught mid-strike, jaw set. The doctor leans in with a small torch, eyebrows up.

mnemonic: On the museum shelf the heart comes first and the lung in the jar comes after it, always after, never before. Lung, jar: lǎng-jàak. Hear the lid click shut on the end of jàak, and remember that หลัง on its own means behind. (↑ lǎng climbs, then jàak drops low and clipped)
headline: lǎng-jàak.
scene: A dim museum shelf of specimen jars. A curator's gloved hand rests on the second jar, which holds a pale lung suspended in fluid; the first jar beside it holds a heart.

mnemonic: He has turned the kitchen out looking for his tea: cupboard doors hanging open, tins on the floor, still no cup. Tea, where? ที่ marks the place and ไหน asks which one, so thîi-nǎi is simply which place. (↓ thîi drops, then nǎi climbs as his eyes come up)
headline: Tea — thîi-nǎi?
scene: A small kitchen turned upside down: every cupboard door hanging open, tins and jars crowding the worktop and the floor. A man stands in the middle of it with both palms turned up and his shoulders raised, staring at an empty shelf.

skip_reason: John-tongue is the only candidate and the ɯ vowel is wrong; nothing in that image carries until.
tip-toe swaps a consonant and teeter has the wrong first vowel; nothing honest fits tìt-tɔ̀ɔ.

mnemonic: A cat stretched the full length of a garden wall lets out a yowl that will not end, one flat note going on and on over the rooftops. Drop the L and there it is: yaao, long. The cat is long and the note is longer. (— dead level; the pitch never moves, it just keeps going)
headline: yaaaao…
scene: A long ginger cat stretched out at full length along the top of a garden wall at night, head back, mouth open in a howl.

mnemonic: A small son stands at the chai stall with his mouth open, following the long ribbon of tea as the vendor pours it from a pot held high into one held low. He has forgotten his own cup entirely. Son, chai: sǒn-jai is exactly that, your attention gone somewhere else. (↑ sǒn climbs, then jai lands flat where his eyes are)
headline: sǒn-jai.
scene: A street chai stall at dusk. A vendor pours a long ribbon of milky tea from a pot held high into another held low, steam curling off it.

mnemonic: The gallery is silent. The artist's arm juts out, the brush touches the huge white canvas once, and that is the whole painting: one black dot in the middle of all that space. jùt is the dot. A jab, and stop. (▁ low and clipped, over as soon as it starts)
headline: jùt.
scene: A white gallery wall holding one enormous blank canvas with a single small black dot at its centre. The artist stands close, arm still thrust forward, a fine brush in hand, the paint still wet.

thai: ยินดีที่ได้รู้จัก
mnemonic: ยินดี yin-dii is gladness: the two halves of the yin symbol clicking together, and ดี dii genuinely does mean good. The tail of the phrase, rúu-jàk, is knowing someone. Glad to have come to know you, and the whole thing lasts exactly one handshake. (— yin-dii sits flat and warm, then the end drops low on jàk)
headline: yin-dii…
scene: Two men meeting in a hotel lobby, hands clasped in a firm handshake, both leaning in slightly, genuinely pleased. Beneath their feet the polished floor carries a large circular inlay of two interlocking black and white teardrops.

mnemonic: Ben swings round with a glass of rye and puts the whole thing down your front. You look at the stain, look at Ben, and wave it away: mâi-bpen-rai. My, Ben, rye. Never mind, it is nothing, it is okay. (↓ mâi drops hard, then the last two float off flat)
headline: mâi-bpen-rai.
scene: A crowded wooden bar. A man has just turned with a tumbler and sloshed dark spirit down the front of another man's shirt; the glass is still tipped in his hand, his face frozen in horror. The soaked man is laughing, one hand raised palm out, entirely unbothered.

mnemonic: The choir stalls seat sixty and three choristers have turned up. They sing the psalm anyway, and the one on the end holds up three fingers to count them all in. Psalm, sǎam, three: the hymn and the number come out of the mouth the same way. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the three fingers)
headline: sǎam.
scene: A vast stone church interior with rows of empty carved choir stalls. Three choristers in red robes stand together in the middle of one row, mouths open in song; the nearest holds up three fingers at chest height.

mnemonic: Six ham hocks hang from six hooks in the butcher's window, and he counts them off along the rail with the back of his knife. Hock, hòk: the meat and the number are the same short syllable, and both stop dead at the k. (▁ low and blunt, cut off at the end)
headline: hòk.
scene: A butcher's window seen from inside the shop: six cured ham hocks hanging in a row from hooks on a steel rail. A butcher in a striped apron runs the back of a knife along them, lips moving as he counts.

mnemonic: The herd files into the milking shed and the farmer counts them through the gate. The ninth cow is always the one that stops in the doorway to think about it, and the gate comes down behind her. Nine cows: gâo. (↓ falling, the gate drops)
headline: gâo.
scene: A milking shed doorway at dusk. Eight cows are already inside the lit shed; the ninth stands square in the open gateway, head turned back, refusing to move. A farmer leans on the gatepost with one hand raised mid-count.

mnemonic: Sun, chart: sǎn-châat. Dawn comes up through the airport hall and the queue holds people dressed for a dozen different countries, every one of them waiting to answer the same question. Which nation are you. That answer is the sǎn-châat. (↑ sǎn climbs, then châat drops flat, like a stamp coming down)
headline: sǎn-châat?
scene: A glass-walled airport hall at sunrise, low orange light stretching across the floor. A long queue of travellers in varied traditional dress — embroidered coats, saris, robes, wool caps — waits at a booth where an officer leans forward with one hand outstretched, palm up.

mnemonic: It is the French word for French, slowed down and given a Thai mouth: français becomes fà-ràng-sèet. The middle of it, farang, is also the everyday Thai word for a Westerner, so France comes out as the farang country. (▁ the first two syllables sit low and short)
headline: fà-ràng-sèet.
scene: A pavement café under a wrought-iron balcony on a grey morning in Paris. A man in a beret plays an accordion beside a round marble table set with coffee and croissants; the great iron tower stands hazy at the end of the street. Wet cobbles, bare plane trees.

mnemonic: Thai cannot begin a word with sp, so it slips a tiny sa in front and comes out with sa-bpeen: Spain, with a step taken in the doorway first. The heel comes down on the tiles and the guitar answers it. (— bpeen stays flat and level, like the long note held under the stamping)
headline: sà-bpeen.
scene: A sunlit whitewashed courtyard. A flamenco dancer in a red ruffled dress is caught mid-stamp, back arched, one arm curved high above her head; a guitarist sits behind her on a wooden chair, head bent over the strings.

mnemonic: The word is already yours, but English says Thai with a dip in the middle of it and the Thai word does not move at all. Hold it dead level from start to finish. ไท also means free, which is why the country reads as the land of the free. (— perfectly flat; no rise, no drop, no dip)
headline: thai.
scene: A wide rice paddy at dawn, the flooded fields lying mirror-flat to the horizon. A farmer in a straw hat stands upright at the edge of the water, arms loose at his sides, looking level at the far bank where a golden temple spire catches the first light.

mnemonic: Three children are digging up the vegetable patch and the noise is tremendous: spades ringing on stone, shrieking, black earth going over the fence. A din. And din is the very stuff they are throwing about, the soil itself. (— flat and level, said as plainly as the ground)
headline: din!
scene: A back garden vegetable patch churned into a crater. Three children with spades fling dark crumbly soil over their shoulders, mouths open in shrieks, earth hanging in the air around them. A dog barks at the edge of the hole.

mnemonic: Nothing is settled until it is tied down. The old sailor takes the rope, finds the exact spot along it and pulls a hard knot into place. Come and knot it, kam-nòt, and now the date exists. It is the word for fixing a thing to a precise point: a deadline, a price, a rule. (— flat on kam, then nòt drops low as the knot pulls tight)
headline: kam-nòt.
scene: Close view of a weathered sailor's hands hauling a thick rope taut and pulling a knot tight at one point along it, the rest of the rope coiling away across the deck planks.

skip_reason: Nothing in English matches pràʔ-maːn; promenade drifts on every syllable and lands on the wrong final consonant.
yacht teaches the open ɔ where Thai has a long o — the one vowel pair learners must not blur.

mnemonic: A jar of jam is wedged under the door and it is the only thing holding the place open: take it away and everything shuts. เป็น bpen means to be, so jam-bpen is what has to be. Not wanted, not nice. Necessary. (— both syllables flat and level; there is nothing to argue with)
headline: jam-bpen.
scene: A heavy wooden door propped open by a squat jar of dark red jam jammed under its bottom edge, the door leaning its weight onto the glass. Beyond it a busy corridor of people passing through.

skip_reason: nan and naan both end in n rather than ŋ, and no English word carries [ɑːŋ] to fix it.
The one close anchor, loam, means soil — it would collide head-on with ดิน in the same batch.
tally has the wrong second vowel (Thai เล is lay), and nothing else in English fits ta-lay.
claw is the wrong vowel for klàːw, and aforementioned cannot be pictured without depicting writing.

mnemonic: โรง is the building — the same โรง that sits in cinema, hotel and factory — and เรียน is to learn. Put the hall and the learning together and school falls out of it: roong-riian, the learning hall. Take โรง away with you; it builds half a town. (— both syllables level and even, like a held bell)
headline: roong-riian.
scene: A school courtyard at morning assembly. Rows of children in white shirts and navy shorts stand in the dust facing a long low building with an open verandah, hands at their sides. A teacher stands at the front with one arm raised.

mnemonic: Tick, and on the tock the coconut lets go. It is a hand's width above the dust now, directly over a man who has slept through the whole business. ตก is anything that falls: rain, prices, a man off a ladder. (▁ low and short, the sound of the landing)
headline: tòk.
scene: Beneath a coconut palm at noon. A large green coconut hangs frozen in the air a hand's width above the dusty ground, right beside a man dozing against the trunk with his hat over his face. A cat is already leaping clear.

skip_reason: The ua diphthong in rùuat has no English match; root and route both flatten it to a plain long u.

mnemonic: The road-mender wipes his forehead with a tarry glove and leaves a perfect black ring round one eye. Everybody who passes looks at that eye and at nothing else on him. dtaa is the eye, and the tar has drawn a circle round it. (— flat and level, an unblinking stare)
headline: dtaa.
scene: Close portrait of a road worker in a high-visibility vest staring straight at the viewer, one eye ringed with a smear of glossy black tar, the glove that did it still raised near his temple.

skip_reason: No English word gives [kʰaj]: chai is the wrong consonant and already anchors จ่าย, and kayak is spent on ขาย.

mnemonic: A phone lies face down in a puddle in the middle of the road, ringing and ringing while the rain hammers it flat, and nobody is coming for it. fǒn is that rain, and the voice climbs the way a ring tone does. (↑ rising, the pitch lifts like a phone waiting to be answered)
headline: fǒn.
scene: A tarmac road in a downpour, seen low and close. A mobile phone lies face down in a shallow puddle, rain bouncing off its back in bright crowns. The street beyond dissolves into grey water and blurred headlights.

mnemonic: A rat is sitting up in the great carved chair at the head of the marble chamber, and the ministers file in and bow to it anyway. Wherever the power happens to be sitting, that is the rát: the state. (▲ high and taut, the way a title is announced)
headline: rát.
scene: A marble parliamentary chamber with columns and tiered benches. A large brown rat sits upright in the ornate carved chair on the raised dais, tail curled over the armrest. Two rows of officials in dark suits bow toward it, heads down.

mnemonic: Some red: the ribbon across the finish line. She takes it on the chest and it snaps and streams back off both shoulders, her arms already up. sǎm-rèt is that exact moment, the thing finished, the thing achieved. Clip the end of red short and the Thai is there. (↑ sǎm climbs, then rèt sits low and clipped as the ribbon breaks)
headline: sǎm-rèt.
scene: A runner breaking a broad red ribbon at a finish line, the ribbon torn and streaming back from her shoulders, both arms flung up, mouth open in a shout. Blurred crowd behind the barriers, other runners far back down the track.

mnemonic: Four men are hammering at a coconut and getting nowhere. The cook walks over, turns it in her palm and opens it with one tap of the cleaver's spine. That is the witty way: wí-thii, the method. A hard t in the middle, never an English th. (— the second syllable holds flat and long, wi-THEE)
headline: wí-thii.
scene: An outdoor kitchen. Four men crouch over a coconut with hammers and a rock, husk fibres scattered everywhere. Beside them a small woman in an apron holds a coconut in one palm, the spine of her cleaver tapping its middle, the shell already opening cleanly in two.

skip_reason: No honest anchor for phaa-sǎa: pasta inserts a t, and nothing else in English comes near it.

mnemonic: Am-purr. Every cat owns a district: the wall, the three roofs and the alley it patrols twice a night, and it sits on the boundary at dusk to look the whole of it over. An amphoe is exactly that, the patch of country belonging to one office. (— both syllables flat and level, like the purr itself)
headline: am-pʰəə.
scene: A large cat sitting upright on a garden wall at dusk, tail curled round its feet, surveying a sprawl of tiled rooftops, alleys and treetops below. Lights are coming on in the houses. Its eyes are half closed and entirely proprietorial.

mnemonic: เดิน is to walk, and it starts like earn with a d pushed in front of it; ทาง is the way, the road. Walk the way and you are travelling: dooen-thaang. The word is not about arriving anywhere, it is the going itself. (— both syllables flat and even, like a steady pace)
headline: dooen-thaang.
scene: A traveller with a heavy pack walking away from the viewer up a red dirt road that winds into green hills.

skip_reason: Four syllables and no English anchor for any of them; anything built here would be invented rather than heard.

mnemonic: At the end of the line the robot arm swings a box down and stacks it onto a wooden pallet, thump, and the pallet fills and another comes up empty behind it. pà-lìt is the making itself: what a factory does all day, every day. (▁ low and flat, the thump of the pallet taking the weight)
headline: pà-lìt.
scene: A factory floor at the end of an assembly line. A yellow robot arm lowers a plain sealed box onto a wooden pallet already stacked shoulder-high with identical boxes; a forklift waits to one side with its forks raised.

mnemonic: พ่อ is PAW, the father, with a round aw in the middle. พา is PAH, with an open ah, and it means to take someone along with you. Here the pa does both: his hand closes round the child's wrist and he tows her through the crowd without breaking stride. (— flat and level, the pace never changes)
headline: pʰaa.
scene: A packed night market seen from behind. A tall father in a work shirt cuts through the crowd with a small girl's wrist held firmly in his hand, her feet skipping to keep up, her free hand clutching a skewer.

skip_reason: Three syllables with no anchor past luck, and the meaning is too abstract to carry a scene on its own.

mnemonic: ผู้ is the one-who, the same ผู้ that starts the words for man and woman, and ใหญ่ is big. An adult is simply the big one: the person who takes the jar off the top shelf without going up on anything. phûu-yài. (↓ phûu drops, then yài settles low, with the weight of being the big one)
headline: phûu-yài.
scene: A kitchen. A small girl up on tiptoe on a stool strains toward a plain jar on the highest shelf, fingers short of it by a foot.

skip_reason: Thai [tɕaːn] needs a long ah: John has the wrong vowel and Jan is too short to teach it.
No English word carries nɛ̀ŋ, and tam on its own cannot hold the word together.
